evidence.claim: Linn Cove carries the Blue Ridge Parkway around Grandfather Mountain on 153 concrete segments.
evidence.quote: The Linn Cove Viaduct is a 1,243-foot-long (379 m), concrete segmental bridge which snakes around Grandfather Mountain

evidence.claim: A crane advanced along the growing bridge, placing each segment from above.
evidence.quote: this was done by connecting 153 segments one at a time using a custom crane that moved along the viaduct as it was being built.

evidence.claim: Almost every segment curves to follow the mountain’s contours.
evidence.quote: All but one of these segments were slightly curved as the viaduct needed to be shaped in a "S-and-a-half" figure to follow the contours of the mountain.

evidence.claim: Blowing Rock takes its name from a cliff above the Johns River Valley, where rising air can return light objects tossed over the edge.
evidence.quote: Blowing Rock, settled in 1870, was named for the nearby cliff rising above the Johns River Valley from which air currents rise and allow light objects to be blown back to the sender.

evidence.claim: The town sits on the crest of the Blue Ridge, with most of it just north of the divide.
evidence.quote: The town is located on the crest of the Blue Ridge. Most of the town lies just north of the crest

evidence.claim: Water on that side drains toward the Middle Fork of the New River and the Ohio River valley.
evidence.quote: with waters draining north to the Middle Fork of the New River and thence to the Ohio River valley

evidence.claim: South of the crest, water reaches the Johns River, then the Catawba valley and eventually the Atlantic in South Carolina.
evidence.quote: while to the south of the ridgecrest, waters flow via the Johns River to the Catawba River valley and eventually to the Atlantic Ocean in South Carolina.

evidence.claim: Linville was established in 1883, with a plan by Samuel T. Kelsey of Kansas.
evidence.quote: Linville, established in 1883 and designed by Samuel T. Kelsey of Kansas, is located on the Linville River.

evidence.claim: At Blowing Rock, the route reaches a town on the Blue Ridge crest, where drainage divides toward the Ohio River valley and the Atlantic.
evidence.quote: The town is located on the crest of the Blue Ridge. Most of the town lies just north of the crest, with waters draining north to the Middle Fork of the New River and thence to the Ohio River valley, while to the south of the ridgecrest, waters flow via the Johns River to the Catawba River valley and eventually to the Atlantic Ocean in South Carolina.

flags: NCDOT cache 23 contains the relevant Little Parkway section; the shorter guidebook copies stop before it despite their page-fragment URLs.

Corrected current viaduct wording: top-down construction did not eliminate all ground work, since the pier footings were drilled from the ground. Kept the Blue Ridge Parkway bridge distinct from the US 221 byway.
Westglow is retained as a documented historic landmark, not a recommendation for its present lodging or spa business. Public interior access is not established.
NCDOT spells the artist Elliott; the Westglow cache uses both Elliott and Elliot. Used NCDOT’s Elliott.
Vehicle advice is checked against the supplied 2021 guide, not live conditions. The cache does not establish current closures or current access to the viaduct.
All other current factual claims were supported somewhere in the cache; the painting detail was omitted to keep Westglow focused on the building.
